weekly_summary:
**Week of October 28, 2026**

Okay so this week felt like everyone collectively decided to stress about the same things at once, processed meat fears and holiday panic. Dr. Berry dropped a video reading through every ingredient on cheap deli meats and hot dogs, basically asking "compared to what?" when people freak out about bologna being deadly. Over 340k views and the comments are full of people saying "I grew up on this stuff and we weren't all sick," which. Yeah, context matters. It's a good reminder that perfect shouldn't be the enemy of good enough, especially if budget is a real factor.

Speaking of not being perfect, I wrote about [getting through the holidays without starting over](/blog/2026-10-27-carnivore-through-the-holidays.html) because I know some of y'all are already sweating Thanksgiving. And if you're dealing with the fatigue that makes holiday prep feel impossible anyway, Sarah's piece on [being tired all the time after 50](/blog/2026-10-26-tired-all-the-time-after-50-carnivore.html) is worth a read. Oh, and exciting news, Sarah posted her first YouTube Shorts! One's about the "only down 3 pounds" frustration in week one, and the other shows how to cook flank steak so it's not chewy shoe leather. We're brand new at this video thing, so [check them out](https://www.youtube.com/@CarnivoreWeekly/shorts) and let us know what you think in the comments or just reply to this newsletter.

Honestly, I keep thinking about how much of this lifestyle is just. Permission to stop overthinking. Eat the hot dog, survive the holidays, don't quit over a weird week on the scale. What's the thing you're currently overthinking?

# Marcus's Analysis: Carnivore Diet YouTube Trends (Week of Oct 21-28, 2026)

## The Big Picture

Alright folks, let me break down what's happening in the carnivore community this week. We've got 27 videos across the space, and Dr. Ken Berry is absolutely dominating with nearly **343,000 views** on a single video about processed meats.

---

## Key Insight #1: The "Processed Meat" Debate is HOT

Dr. Berry's video "Processed Meats Will Kill You? I read every ingredient" is crushing it right now.

**Why this matters to you:**
- **11,379 likes** and **1,438 comments** shows massive engagement
- People are hungry (pun intended) for permission to eat affordable meats
- The budget angle is resonating hard

**Actionable takeaway:** If you're creating content or just living this lifestyle, lean into the "carnivore on a budget" angle. Hot dogs, bologna, and deli meats are clearly topics people want defended.

---

## Key Insight #2: Nostalgia is a Powerful Hook

Look at the top comments:

> *"This is all stuff we ate in the 80s and we were not a fat society"*,  339 likes

> *"I grew up poor and this is all the food I ate"*,  304 likes

**The pattern:** People are connecting processed meats to a time before obesity epidemics. This "grandma's kitchen" framing is resonating emotionally.

**For you:** When defending your carnivore choices to skeptics, try: *"These foods fed healthy generations before us. What changed was the seed oils and sugar, not the bacon."*

---

## Key Insight #3: "Compared to WHAT?" is the Winning Framework

That truncated third comment hits on Berry's signature move,  demanding context. Processed meat compared to what? Doritos? Kale smoothies with 40g sugar?

**Use this:** Next time someone criticizes your food choices, flip it: *"Compared to what most Americans eat for breakfast, my sausage links are practically medicine."*

---

## What Should You Watch This Week?

Start with that Berry video if you haven't already. The ingredient breakdown format is educational and shareable.

qa_section.question: What should people know about processed meat safety on a carnivore diet?
qa_section.answer:
Before we dive in, how are you feeling about your carnivore journey so far? I want to make sure we're addressing what's actually on your mind.

Processed meats like bacon, deli meats, and sausages contain sodium nitrites and nitrates, which have raised health concerns in observational studies. Research shows associations between high processed meat consumption and increased cardiovascular risk in large population studies. However, here's what matters for context: most of this research comes from people eating processed meat alongside refined carbohydrates, seed oils, and ultra-processed foods. The carnivore context is different. On a meat-based diet, you're removing the inflammatory load that typically accompanies processed meat consumption in standard diets. That said, quantity and quality still matter. Unprocessed muscle meat remains your foundation for a reason.

If you're tracking blood glucose markers or using a continuous glucose monitor, you'll notice processed meats have minimal impact on glucose stability compared to their carb-containing counterparts. People report feeling fine on them short-term. The real question becomes about long-term sodium load and whether the additives matter at your intake levels. Some people do better rotating in fresh beef, organs, and unprocessed options most of the time, treating processed meats as occasional foods rather than dietary staples. Pay attention to how your body responds. Your Oura or Whoop data around sleep quality and HRV can actually tell you something useful here. If you notice sleep disruption or elevated resting heart rate correlated with high processed meat days, that's valuable personal data worth adjusting for.

The honest take: processed meat on carnivore isn't the same risk profile as processed meat in a standard diet, but it's also not a free-pass food. Use it strategically. Your healing comes from consistency with whole muscle meats first, not from finding ways to maximize convenience foods.

citations.authors: Bechthold A, Boeing H, Schwedhelm C, et al.

qa_section.caveats: The research on processed meat comes primarily from observational studies in omnivorous populations eating high-carb, high-seed-oil diets. Direct studies on processed meat in strict carnivore contexts are limited. Individual response varies significantly based on sodium sensitivity, inflammatory status, and overall meat quality. Sodium content in processed meats may be a consideration for people with blood pressure sensitivity. The absence of other processed foods and plant seed oils in carnivore eating may meaningfully reduce some risks associated with processed meat in conventional diets, but this remains an area where personal experimentation and biomarker tracking matter more than universal recommendations.

qa_section.question: What should people know about budget carnivore eating on a carnivore diet?
qa_section.answer:
Here's the real talk on budget carnivore: you don't need to drop serious cash to run this protocol. The ROI equation is simple. Cheap protein sources like ground beef, organ meats, and eggs deliver the same nutrient density as premium cuts. Your body doesn't care if that beef came from a butcher's premium case or the markdown bin. What matters is the protein-to-dollar ratio and whether you're consistent.

The playbook: buy in bulk when prices drop, source ground beef and chuck roasts instead of steaks, grab organ meats (liver, kidney, heart) which are dirt cheap and nutrient-dense, and hit up ethnic markets where beef tends to be priced better. Eggs remain one of the most cost-efficient protein sources on the planet. Research on protein adequacy shows that meeting your protein targets matters way more than the source of those proteins. A 2019 analysis in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition found that diverse protein sources achieve similar satiety and metabolic outcomes when total intake matches your needs.

Here's what separates winners from quitters: consistency beats perfection every single time. Someone eating budget ground beef and eggs consistently will see better results than someone chasing grass-fed premium meats sporadically. Track your protein intake, lock in your budget per week, and automate your shopping list (spreadsheet or even a simple n8n workflow to flag sales at your local stores). The difference between success and failure on carnivore isn't usually the quality tier. It's showing up and executing the protocol week after week.

qa_section.caveats: The research on budget versus premium protein sources within a carnivore context is limited, so we're extrapolating from broader protein science and ketogenic/low-carb diet literature. Micronutrient density does vary by cut and animal part (organ meats have advantages over muscle meat), so diversifying your protein sources within your budget makes sense. Individual digestion and tolerance can vary, so you may need to experiment with different cheap sources to find what works for your gut. Availability of budget options depends on location and season. The key limitation: no randomized controlled trials directly compare budget versus premium carnivore protocols, so this answer relies on mechanistic understanding and real-world application.

qa_section.question: What should people know about carnivore on a budget on a carnivore diet?
qa_section.answer:
Listen, carnivore on a budget isn't some fantasy scenario. It's actually your highest-ROI move if you play it smart. Here's the reality: meat prices fluctuate wildly by cut and source. Fatty cuts like chuck roast, ground beef, and organ meats (liver, kidney, heart) run 40-60% cheaper than ribeye while delivering superior micronutrient density. You're getting more bang for your buck nutritionally. Eggs are your secret weapon here too. At roughly $0.20-0.40 per egg depending on region, they're the cheapest complete protein on the market. Buy in bulk, buy on sale, buy the less trendy cuts. Your grocery strategy matters more than your macros do.

The budget play gets real when you eliminate food waste and spontaneous purchases. Carnivore is naturally satiating due to high protein and fat intake, which means fewer snacking episodes and smaller overall food budgets compared to standard diets. Research on ketogenic diets shows adherents typically experience reduced food cravings and improved appetite control, which translates directly to fewer trips to the store and less money bleeding out on impulse buys. You're automating your food choices, which frees up decision-making bandwidth and cash. Focus on ground beef, eggs, cheaper organ meats, and full-fat dairy if you tolerate it. Skip the premium grass-fed marketing unless your budget allows it. Conventional beef gets the job done.

Here's what matters: consistency beats perfection. A $3/day carnivore budget beats a $10/day mixed diet every single time because you stay on track. That's the ROI equation. The micronutrient profile of organ meats on budget is legitimately superior to what most people eating conventionally get for the same price. This isn't deprivation. This is strategic resource allocation.

qa_section.caveats: Budget carnivore requires discipline on sourcing. Quality varies significantly by retailer, so comparing prices per pound across multiple sources pays off fast. Regional differences in meat pricing are substantial. Ground beef prices can swing $2-5/pound depending on location and season. Organ meats spoil faster than muscle meat, so buying smaller quantities more frequently is often smarter than bulk purchasing. There's limited direct research comparing carnivore diets specifically at different price points, but the satiety research on protein and low-carb approaches strongly supports the budget efficiency argument. Individual tolerance to organ meats varies, so start conservative. The budget advantage disappears if you're buying premium grass-fed everything. That's a luxury tier, not a necessity. Conventional meat works fine.
